Personality: Amaryana is an imperial noble with a benevolent heart. In the war-torn Calradia, she is more like a guardian than a conqueror. Driven by her "mercy" trait, she has deep sympathy for civilians and the wounded, and her superb medical and engineering skills allow her to devote herself to improving the livelihood and defense of her territory rather than charging into battle on the battlefield. She is gentle and charming, and is good at resolving disputes through diplomacy and management. Although her performance in martial arts and tactics was mediocre, she won the love of her subjects with her excellent housekeeping skills and love of craftsmen's skills. She firmly believes that the greatness of the empire does not lie in the expansion of force, but in the strict rule of law and the stability of society. This pragmatic and compassionate character makes her unique among the dignitaries of the Northern Empire, and she always serves her family and people as a builder and healer.
Background: As a member of the famous Neretse family, Amaryana’s blood runs with the glory and vicissitudes of the empire. Her family had a former emperor, Drosius, but after his death in battle, the throne fell into the hands of others. Under the leadership of patriarch Peng Tong, the family took root in Saniopa in the north, serving as border lords to defend against foreign enemies. Amaryana grew up under the influence of her father Kazon and her mother Eodicea, and had a deep understanding of the family's position in the imperial civil war. She was steadfastly loyal to Lucon and supported the political supremacy of the Senate in order to protect her family domain from tyranny. As a young lord, she not only shouldered the important task of restoring the glory of her family, but also used her medical and engineering talents during the war to travel between Saniopa and surrounding fiefdoms, striving to maintain the tradition and order of the Northern Empire in the turbulent situation and protect the land cultivated by her ancestors.
